Violence conjugale – après les bleus, la: Domestic violence – after the bruises, the fear of losing their children
Trois mères disent avoir dénoncé la viol: Three mothers say they reported domestic violence, only to see their situation reframed as “parental conflict.”
<strong>Elles ont osé dénoncer la violen: They dared to report domestic violence. Some say that afterwards their word was called into question, their bonds with their children grew strained, or their situation was interpreted through the lens of “parental conflict.” Through the stories of three mothers, the analysis of researchers and the response of the DPJ, La Converse explores an institutional blind spot: those situations where domestic violence and child protection collide.
Autour de la table, dans les bureaux de: Around the table, in La Converse’s offices, three women tell their stories, which share many similarities and are marked by the same pain. Only one agrees to be identified. The other two ask for anonymity, fearing reprisals despite years of legal proceedings.
La première à prendre la parole est Ange: The first to speak is Angela*. She hasn’t seen her children in nine years. Nine years of absence, with no birthdays, no Christmases, no family photos. Nine years without being able to talk to them. “The worst thing you can do to a mother isn’t to take her life, it’s to take her children,” she says, her gaze sad.
Ce qui ne devait être qu’une séparation: What was supposed to be just a separation turned into a tragedy. A tragedy that now affects three generations. Her own mother died without ever having held her grandchildren in her arms, and the grandchildren, in turn, did not attend their grandmother’s funeral. These words leave the room silent. “I’m no longer fighting just for my children. I’m fighting for my future grandchildren,” says Angela.
Pour Alice* et Manon*, témoigner demeure: For Alice* and Manon*, speaking out remains a high-risk exercise. Both mothers fear reviving a legal battle that already poisons their daily lives, and dread the effects on their careers.
Les décisions rendues dans leurs dossier: The decisions handed down in their cases are not the same, and their family contexts are also different. Yet one feeling runs through all their accounts: all three say they had the impression that the violence they were reporting gradually stopped being at the centre of the discussions, to be replaced by other considerations and other
expressions comme « conflit parental »,: expressions such as “parental conflict,” “severe separation conflict” or “toxic relationship.”
« Tout ce que je dénonçais comme de la v: “Everything I was reporting as violence, at some point, became a parental conflict,” Alice sums up. For her, this shift profoundly changed her perception of the consequences a report can have. “Do you think a lot of mothers are going to report abuse if they know they risk losing their children?” Angela asks. The other women nod. Alice then says something that freezes
l’atmosphère : « Si j’avais su que j’all: the atmosphere: “If I had known I was going to lose my children, I would have put up with the violence rather than report it.”
Une grande question demeure : comment le: One big question remains: how do institutions tell a conflict apart from a situation of coercive control?
Dans le récit de Manon, la protection de: In Manon’s account, youth protection entered the case after one of her daughters went through a serious crisis. She says she discovered, in the child’s diary, passages describing physical violence by her father, and filed a new complaint with police. According to her account, police then contacted the DPJ, which became more directly involved in the case.
Manon affirme avoir remis à la DPJ une e: Manon says she gave the DPJ a psychosocial assessment, police reports and a document of about fifty pages in which she set out, among other things, the psychological, verbal and financial abuse she said she had endured. Yet she maintains that the official assessment report concluded there was a “separation conflict,” without treating violence as a central element. She says she then felt her role had been reversed: instead of being regarded as a mother trying to protect her children, she now had to justify herself.
Pour ces femmes, cette crainte constitue: For these women, this fear is one of the blind spots in the public debate on the issue. Awareness campaigns encourage victims to leave violent relationships and report abuse. But, in their view, some of the consequences of doing so remain largely unknown.
Les trois mères affirment avoir agi dans: The three mothers say they acted in their children’s best interests, trying to protect them. The system was set in motion: courts, psychosocial assessments, motions, appeals. The psychological toll was compounded by financial ruin. Alice says she sank more than $200,000 into legal fees. “Legal aid exists, but as soon as you earn a decent salary, you’re no longer eligible. To get through it, you need colossal means.”
Dans le cas d’Angela, comme la résidence: In Angela’s case, because the family home was owned by both spouses, she was not eligible for legal aid, despite her financial situation as an unemployed mother. “I was billed more than $1,000,000,” she says of the fees she had to pay over the years. To get through this ordeal, she had to rely on help from her parents.
The word “exhaustion” comes up again and again. The feeling that the case never fully closes. And all the while, time (and childhood) slip by.
Aux dires du professeur Simon Lapierre,: According to Professor Simon Lapierre, a domestic violence specialist at the University of Ottawa, these are not isolated cases. “[There is a] confusion between domestic violence and separation conflict, but above all the fact that situations of post-separation domestic violence are perceived or interpreted as parental conflict or separation conflict,” the researcher points out. In his view, this confusion stems first from an
compréhension encore incomplète de la vi: still-incomplete understanding of domestic violence. “There’s still this tendency to think that domestic violence is something that happens when the parents live together, when the parents are still together. And then, once the couple has separated, it’s no longer domestic violence,” he illustrates.
Il y a aussi l’image que plusieurs se fo: There is also the image many people still have of domestic violence: that of a physically brutal man facing a woman bearing obvious signs of abuse. But not all violence leaves visible marks. Control, coercive hold, surveillance and psychological violence can be much harder to recognize and to distinguish from the various aspects of a relationship that is simply conflictual. Yet, Lapierre explains, reality very often doesn’t fit that model. “When situations don’t match that vision of domestic violence – because it isn’t necessarily physical violence, or there was very little physical violence, or the perpetrator is charming and likable, or the victim maybe doesn’t ‘look like a victim’ – we’ll sometimes conclude it’s a conflict.”
Pour Simon Lapierre, cette façon de voir: For Simon Lapierre, this way of seeing things often obscures a reality that is nonetheless widely documented by research: coercive control. Far from being a series of isolated incidents, this form of violence rests on a set of behaviours aimed at controlling the other parent, monitoring them or restricting their freedom over a long period. “Domestic violence,” he specifies, “is not the result of one or a few incidents of violence. It’s rather that one person uses all kinds of strategies over time to control the other partner and deprive them of their freedom.”
À cela s’ajoutent parfois des considérat: Sometimes, vaguer considerations come on top of this. “Separation conflict sometimes becomes the default category when you can’t prove there is domestic violence,” the researcher observes.
La distinction n’est pas toujours simple: The distinction between conflict and violence in a couple isn’t always simple. “If we had a simple answer to that question, I think we could retire,” says Catherine Turbide, a professor at the Université du Québec à Rimouski.
Avec sa collègue Élisabeth Godbout, de l: With her colleague Élisabeth Godbout, of Université Laval, she is currently conducting research aimed at better understanding the realities hiding behind separation conflicts and post-separation domestic violence. The two researchers note that some of the manifestations seen in family case files can look alike, including persistent hostility between the parents, a proliferation of court proceedings, difficulty communicating and disputes over the children. “These characteristics don’t let us say, ‘There you go, if we have these criteria, we’re dealing with conflict,’ because these same characteristics could also be observed in contexts of violence,” explains Ms.<sup></sup> Turbide.
Il faut donc regarder au-delà des compor: So we have to look beyond visible behaviours. “When we talk about post-separation domestic violence, we’re talking about a really particular type of dynamic,” she continues. “There’s one parent who is a victim of the other parent; there’s a power imbalance between the two. We’re talking about control strategies, about coercive control.”
M<sup>me</sup> Turbide souligne égalemen: Ms.<sup></sup> Turbide also stresses that family trajectories are rarely simple. Some victims don’t reveal right away what they went through, and others realize only over time that certain behaviours amount to domestic violence. “Sometimes they don’t even realize that’s what happened. It comes later in the process,” adds
Or, une fois qu’une évaluation est termi: Yet once an assessment is finished or a decision is handed down, it’s hard to go back. “We need a certain flexibility, and again, space, resources, time, because if we want a victim to report what they’ve been through, we have to be able to maintain a connection with that person,” she concludes.
Les conséquences d’une mauvaise lecture: The consequences of misreading a situation of domestic violence can be significant, particularly when children are involved, Simon Lapierre argues. If a situation of domestic violence is interpreted as mere parental conflict, “we won’t do a proper assessment of the danger or even the risk of homicide,” he says.
Selon le chercheur, les signaux d’alarme: According to the researcher, the alarm signals raised by mothers can then be seen as excessive or unjustified. “Rather than taking it seriously and saying, ‘OK, what makes you afraid? Can we investigate further?’, we risk dismissing that fear
du revers de la main », résume-t-il. Le: out of hand,” he sums up. The same phenomenon can affect children, he goes on: “When the child cries because he doesn’t want to go see his father, [...] we risk saying that he’s being exposed to conflict or that his mother has influenced his point of view.”
Élisabeth Godbout partage l’idée que les: Élisabeth Godbout shares the view that children’s reactions must be examined carefully. She also urges caution, however. “We have to go beyond the child’s resistance to understand the multiple causes that push them to act that way,” she says, stressing that there is no single explanation for the refusals of contact expressed by some children. Sometimes these reactions may be linked to violence experienced
ou observée, et parfois, elles peuvent d: or witnessed, and sometimes they may stem from other family dynamics. She also warns against certain preconceptions that can influence how cases are interpreted. “Often, a parent who is abusive will present well, be articulate, be in control of the situation, look like the good, responsible parent,” Élisabeth Godbout points out. Conversely, a person who has experienced trauma may seem confused, emotional or less coherent.
Pour Catherine Turbide, mettre en œuvre: For Catherine Turbide, implementing interventions designed for parental conflicts in a situation of domestic violence can have heavy consequences. “The risk,” she says, “is to revictimize these women, and to put young people back in situations where they’re exposed to violence.”
Si les deux chercheuses reconnaissent le: While both researchers acknowledge the progress made in recent years, they believe institutions still need time, resources and tools to respond better to these complex situations.
Élisabeth Godbout souligne que des forma: Élisabeth Godbout points out that training is currently being rolled out and that the recent<l1> legislative changes</l1> give practitioners more guidance. But she remains cautious. “It’s far from perfect.” Ms.<sup></sup> Godbout and Turbide are also taking part in a major action research project aimed at adapting socio-judicial interventions to the different realities of post-separation domestic violence. Their goal is to reduce the risks of
revictimisation et de mieux protéger les: revictimization and to better protect the families affected.
En attendant, elles défendent une approc: In the meantime, they advocate an approach based on the precautionary principle. “When in doubt, it’s better to add more safety than less,” says Élisabeth Godbout. In her view, society rightly places great importance on maintaining ties between children and both their parents after a separation. In some situations, however, the priority shouldn’t be rebuilding the parental bond but protecting the people involved, she believes. “We have to ask: at what price are we maintaining contact?”
<strong>Vers un changement de culture à: Toward a culture change at the DPJ?
Comment la DPJ voit-elle aujourd’hui ces: How does the DPJ view these situations today? Hélène Groleau, director of youth protection services, diversity and First Nations and Inuit communities at the Ministry of Health and Social Services, begins by acknowledging the complexity of these cases. “These are extremely complex family situations,” she says.
M<sup>me </sup>Groleau rappelle qu’en 20: Ms.<sup> </sup>Groleau recalls that in 2022, the<l1> Youth Protection Act</l1> was amended to explicitly recognize children’s exposure to domestic violence as a distinct ground for intervention. The reform aimed in particular to take better account of
post-séparation. « On est aussi venu ret: post-separation situations. “We also removed a criterion that existed before, namely that the facts had to be serious or ongoing. The objective,” she specifies, “was to give the Director of Youth Protection every possible lever to protect children.” The director also acknowledges that practices needed to evolve.
Dans la foulée de ces changements, un gu: In the wake of these changes, a ministerial guide was developed with women’s groups, community organizations and researchers, among them Professor Simon Lapierre. According to the ministry, several thousand practitioners have received training on the new legislative provisions, and specialized training is now offered across Quebec.
‍<strong>Le contrôle coercitif au cœur d: ‍Coercive control at the heart of the changes
À l’instar des chercheurs rencontrés par: Like the researchers La Converse spoke with, Hélène Groleau considers coercive control a central element in distinguishing domestic violence from parental conflict. “It’s truly the distinguishing element […] Our ministerial guidelines have embraced the concept of coercive control more fully,” she says, pointing to the unequal power dynamic that sets in in some relationships and can continue after separation. Although it now has an important place in the clinical guides used by the DPJ, the concept hasn’t been written directly into the law.
Interrogée sur les critiques formulées p: Asked about criticism from some mothers and several researchers of interventions focused on co-parenting (processes meant to get separated parents to cooperate better in their children’s interests), she also acknowledges the risks. In a context of post-separation domestic violence, she explains, practitioners who run these programs may assume there is a relatively equal relationship between the two parents, when one of them may continue to exert control over the other. “These programs must be avoided for women who are victims of post-separation domestic violence, because of the far too great risk that the process will be instrumentalized.”
Enfin, la directrice se dit « attristée: Finally, the director says she is “saddened” to hear that some women today are afraid to report violence for fear of losing their children. “What you’re describing is the last thing we want.”
M<sup>me </sup>Groleau affirme que le so: Ms.<sup> </sup>Groleau says support for the non-violent parent remains an essential element of protecting children and argues for better coordination among the DPJ, the courts, police, community organizations and specialized services in order to limit revictimization. “If at least the systems allow victims to repeat their
moins souvent possible leur histoire, on: story as seldom as possible, then we’re really moving forward,” she says, expressing the wish to synchronize socio-judicial processes more in order to minimize the impact on victims and families in general.
Du côté des maisons d’hébergement, la ré: At domestic violence shelters, the reality remains raw. Florence*, a worker at a shelter for women who are victims of domestic violence, sees this terror of reporting every day, particularly among mothers with immigrant backgrounds. Precarious status, language barriers, economic isolation: too often, the system turns these women into “non-protective mothers.”
Elle explique que les maisons d’hébergem: She explains that shelters carry out their own assessments to distinguish situations of domestic violence from parental conflicts.
Pourtant, dit-elle, cette lecture n’est: Yet, she says, this reading isn’t always taken up by all institutions. “When you enter the justice system or certain youth protection processes, domestic violence can be denied. It may not be recognized at all.” The consequences she sees in women are many: psychological exhaustion, financial insecurity, loss of trust in institutions and a feeling of no longer being heard. “Many end up abandoning certain claims or lowering their expectations because they no longer have the energy to keep going.”
Elle souligne le poids particulier que c: She stresses the particular burden these women must carry: “These victims are said to be non-protective [of their children], when they are often mothers who are completely destitute.”
Comme Hélène Groleau de la DPJ, Florence: Like the DPJ’s Hélène Groleau, Florence believes that better coordination among institutions is one of the main challenges. “The shelter deals with the woman, the DPJ with the children, criminal court with the aggressor, family court with custody. But there’s no place where everyone sits down together,” the shelter worker laments. In her view, this
fragmentation peut faire en sorte que ce: fragmentation can cause some families to “fall through the cracks,” because “[we] all work with the same family, but each of us acts on our own.”
Ces changements de pratiques s’inscriven: These changes in practice are part of a broader legislative debate. In Quebec, Sherbrooke MNA Christine Labrie tabled Bill 598 in April 2026, Loi visant à protéger l’enfant et le parent victimes de violence familiale. The text proposes, among other things, no longer presuming that joint exercise of parental authority is in the child’s best interests. It would also create a presumption against granting custody to a parent found to have committed family violence, unless that parent can show that custody is in the child’s interests and that measures exist to ensure the other parent’s safety and stop the violence. The bill also provides that certain unproven allegations of violence and certain behaviours adopted by a parent to protect themselves or their child cannot, on their own, be held against them in custody decisions.
Le débat existe aussi à Ottawa. Le proje: The debate is also taking place in Ottawa. Federal Bill C-223,<l1> Keeping Children Safe Act</l1>, introduced in 2025 and passed at second reading in February 2026, is currently being studied in committee. It proposes amending the Divorce Act to better take family violence and coercive control into account, notably when courts assess relationships between a child and their parents. The text also addresses situations where a parent is accused of trying to damage the child’s relationship with the other parent.
Aucun de ces projets n’est encore une lo: Neither of these bills is law yet. But their existence reflects a shared concern: preventing a parent’s behaviours aimed at ensuring their own or their child’s safety from being automatically interpreted, in a context of family violence, as an obstacle to the relationship with the other parent.
Neuf ans après avoir vu ses enfants pour: Nine years after last seeing her children, Angela continues to hope that one day they will hear her version of the story. Between the mothers’ accounts, the researchers’ work and the institutions’ responses, one question remains: how can we make sure that protecting children never comes at the price of making the reported violence invisible?
La reconnaissance dans la loi ne règle p: Recognition in law doesn’t settle everything.
Les données les plus récentes indiquent: The most recent data show that children’s exposure to domestic violence now accounts for a significant share of youth protection interventions. According to the<l1> 2024-2025 annual report of the directors of youth protection</l1>, a quarter of children taken into care in Quebec are there because of psychological maltreatment or exposure to domestic violence. Since April 2023, this type of violence has in fact been a distinct ground for a finding that a child’s security or development is compromised under the Youth Protection Act, whereas it was previously listed among forms of psychological maltreatment.
Ces données ne permettent toutefois pas: However, these data do not allow for a direct parallel with the three mothers La Converse spoke to. Their cases predate these figures, are different, and are part of complex judicial and institutional trajectories. All three maintain, however, that the domestic violence they reported was gradually pushed to the background or reclassified as “parental conflict” or a separation conflict, a dynamic that is precisely one of the issues examined in this report.
Au cours de la dernière année, la DPJ a: Over the past year, the DPJ processed 141,662 reports in Quebec. Of these, nearly 41,500 were accepted for evaluation. Young children remain the most likely to be the subject of an intervention: 35.3% of reports concerning children aged 0 to 5 are accepted, compared with 20.3% of those concerning teenagers aged 16 and 17. Reports come mainly from professionals. Police account for 24.6% of the reports processed, schools for 24.1%, and various organizations and institutions in the network for 31.8%. Reports from police forces have nearly doubled over the past 10 years.
